name: Painted Grey Ware culture
info: The Painted Grey Ware culture, named by archaeologists after its fine grey pottery painted in black, was an Iron Age culture of the western Gangetic plain and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley in northern India, c. 1200–600 BCE.

facts.homeland: The western Gangetic plain and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley, with the Sutlej and upper Ganga-Yamuna valleys (Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh, around Delhi); key sites Mathura, Ahichhatra, Jakhera, Bhagwanpura, Alamgirpur, Kampil
facts.period: Conventionally c. 1200–600/500 BCE, or 1300–500/300 BCE; Akinori Uesugi’s Period I c. 1300–1000 BCE, Period II c. 1000–600 BCE, Period III c. 600–300 BCE; earlier radiocarbon dates have been reported from single sites
facts.known: fine grey drinking ware painted with black geometric patterns; early iron metallurgy in the region; farming villages and some fortified towns; domesticated horses; ivory-working; stamp seals without inscriptions
facts.sources: Excavated sites (1,576 known as of 2018) and surveys; radiocarbon dates; the later Vedic literature, which the culture probably corresponds to

t: Painted Grey Ware is an archaeologists’ name for a culture identified by its fine grey bowls painted with simple black patterns, found at 1,576 sites in northern India.
Its people farmed with the plough, kept cattle, sheep, pigs and horses, worked iron and ivory, and lived mostly in villages, with several dozen towns.
It probably corresponds to the middle and late Vedic period and the Kuru-Panchala kingdom, and many of its settlements grew into the towns of the Northern Black Polished Ware period.
dyk: The painted grey ware was a luxury: almost all of it is drinking ware, and it makes up only 10–15% of the pottery found from Vedic times, most of the rest being red ware.
ev: Painted Grey Ware appears in the Ghaggar valley and the upper Ganga region (Uesugi’s Period I)
The culture spreads into the western part of the Ganga valley (Uesugi’s Period II)
Northern Black Polished Ware succeeds it, with the rise of the Mahajanapada states
In Uesugi’s Period III the culture interacts with regions to the east
Plain Grey Ware is found at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka in levels of 600–500 BCE, showing connections with northern India
Excavations at Alamgirpur, near Delhi, reveal an overlap between late Harappan and the earliest Painted Grey Ware levels
Two periods of Painted Grey Ware are identified at Ahichhatra, c. 1500–800 and 800–400 BCE
1,576 Painted Grey Ware sites are known

sections.origins:
The Painted Grey Ware culture (PGW) is an archaeologists’ name, taken from its most distinctive find: a fine, grey pottery painted with geometric patterns in black. It belongs to the Iron Age of the western Gangetic plain and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley, and is conventionally dated c. 1200 to 600–500 BCE, or by others from 1300 to 500–300 BCE. In this region it succeeded the Cemetery H culture and the Black and Red Ware culture, which continued in the eastern Gangetic plain and Central India.

The archaeologist Akinori Uesugi divides it into three periods: Period I (c. 1300–1000 BCE), when it appears in the Ghaggar valley and the upper Ganga region; Period II (c. 1000–600 BCE), when it spreads into the western Ganga valley; and Period III (c. 600–300 BCE), with interactions to the east. Some excavations have given much earlier dates: two periods at Ahichhatra from c. 1500 BCE, PGW levels at Kampil published as 2310 ± 120 and 1360 ± 90 BCE, and a layer at Alamgirpur, near Delhi, where late Harappan and the earliest PGW levels overlap, dated to 1647 BCE.

Who made it is debated. The culture is described as Indo-Aryan and loosely linked with the early Aryans thought to have migrated into India at the beginning of the Vedic period. Its pottery differs from that of the Iranian Plateau and Afghanistan, and at some sites it is contemporary with Late Harappan pottery. The archaeologist Jim Shaffer noted that the record shows “no cultural discontinuities” separating it from the indigenous protohistoric culture; others answer that potters were generally local craftsmen even after the Indo-Aryan migration. According to D. K. Chakrabarti and other scholars, its subsistence patterns, such as the use of rice, and most of its other features originated in eastern India or even Southeast Asia.
sections.society:
Most PGW sites were small farming villages. People grew rice, wheat, millet and barley, using the plough, and kept cattle, sheep, pigs and horses. Houses were built of wattle and daub, mud or brick, from small huts to large houses with many rooms. As population grew, settlements multiplied in number and size, with a clear hierarchy of a few central towns among many villages.

“Several dozen” sites grew into towns. The largest were fortified with ditches or moats and embankments of piled earth with wooden palisades, smaller and simpler than the defences of the cities built after 600 BCE. Jakhera in Uttar Pradesh shows a “fairly evolved, proto-urban or semi-urban stage”, with ornaments of gold, copper, ivory and semi-precious stones, storage bins for surplus grain, stone weights, paved streets, water channels and embankments. New surveys by Vinay Kumar Gupta suggest that Mathura, at around 375 hectares, was the largest PGW site; Ahichhatra covered at least 40 hectares and had early fortifications.

At Bhagwanpura in the Kurukshetra district of Haryana, large houses may have been the homes of an elite. For the period 1000–600 BCE, George Erdosy found a two-tiered pattern of settlements in the Ganges Valley, with some modest central places suggesting simple chiefdoms, and a more complex three-tiered pattern in the Kurukshetra district itself.
sections.beliefs:
Its few stamp seals bear geometric designs but no inscription, unlike both the earlier Harappan seals and the later Brahmi-inscribed seals of the Northern Black Polished Ware culture, so its beliefs must be inferred from objects. Incised terracotta discs with decorated edges and geometric motifs probably had a “ritual meaning”, perhaps as symbols of deities, and terracotta figurines of humans and animals have also been found. At Bhagwanpura, fired bricks may have been used in Vedic altars.

If the culture corresponds, as it probably does, to the middle and late Vedic period, the later Vedic literature gives a mass of information on the life of the time. The Kuru kingdom, with which it is associated, systematised the Vedic religious literature and developed the Śrauta ritual of sacrifice.
sections.arts:
The pottery that names the culture is highly standardised. It is wheel-thrown to a smooth, ash-grey finish and painted in black, most often with vertical, oblique or criss-cross lines, rows of dots, spiral chains and concentric circles; swastikas and sigma shapes also occur. Bowls of two shapes dominate, a shallow tray and a deeper bowl, often with a sharp angle between wall and base. The grey ware is almost all drinking ware, in tall narrow-waisted glasses, middle-sized goblets and vases with out-turned lips, and it was a “highly valued luxury”: it makes up only 10–15% of the pottery found from Vedic times.

The culture is associated with the advent of iron metallurgy in its region, and the groups who made the pottery are thought to have brought iron technology to the Indo-Gangetic plains. When iron first came into use in northern India is itself debated: Rakesh Tewari has dated furnaces, tuyeres and slag in Uttar Pradesh to c. 1800–1000 BCE, while Suraj Bhan found the context and chronology of those finds “not beyond doubt”, though he had no doubt that iron was in use in the Ganges Plain a few centuries before the rise of cities around 600 BCE. Other crafts included ivory-working and ornaments of terracotta, stone, faience and glass.
sections.exchange:
The PGW culture belonged to a wider world of pottery cultures. In the western Ganges plain it followed the Black and Red Ware, and in some sites its pottery is contemporary with Late Harappan wares; at Bhagwanpura the late Harappan and PGW cultures overlap. It did not expand east of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab. There a related but markedly different culture of the central Ganges region developed, associated with the Northern Black Polished Ware and the kingdoms of Kosala and Magadha.

Ornaments of gold, ivory and semi-precious stones, and stone weights, at Jakhera point to trade. Far to the south, excavation at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka in 2006 found Plain Grey Ware, the ware associated in northern India with Painted Grey Ware, in the town’s basal early historic levels of 600–500 BCE, showing connections with northern India. In its last period, according to Uesugi, the culture interacted with the regions to its east.
sections.legacy:
Towards the end of the period many PGW settlements grew into the large towns and cities of the Northern Black Polished Ware period. That culture succeeded PGW around 700–500 BCE and is associated with the rise of the great Mahajanapada states and of the Magadha Empire; the fortified cities built after 600 BCE were far more elaborate than the PGW towns had been.

The culture probably corresponds to the middle and late Vedic period, the time of the Kuru-Panchala kingdom, the first large state in the Indian subcontinent after the decline of the Indus Valley Civilisation. New work goes on adding sites and dates, from the excavations at Ahichhatra, Kampil and Alamgirpur to the surveys around Mathura.

summary: The Painted Grey Ware culture is an archaeologists’ name for an Iron Age culture of the western Gangetic plain and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley, c. 1200–600 BCE, named after its fine grey pottery painted in black. Its people farmed with the plough, kept horses, worked iron and ivory, and lived in villages and some towns. It probably corresponds to the later Vedic Kuru-Panchala kingdom and was followed by the cities of the Northern Black Polished Ware period.

notes: Dates kept at -1200/-600 as assigned (the conventional dating). The article gives alternatives: “600–500 BCE” as the end, 1300–500/300 BCE, and Uesugi’s three periods to c. 300 BCE; the Vedic article has 1200–600 BCE. Single-site radiocarbon dates (Ahichhatra from c. 1500 BCE, Kampil 2310 ± 120 BCE, Alamgirpur 1647 BCE, Gosna 2160/2170 BCE) are reported in the text as results, not as the culture’s dates; Gosna left out (the article says its PGW association is lost).

Identity: the article calls PGW an “Indo-Aryan culture” and says it “probably corresponds” to the middle and late Vedic period; Shaffer’s continuity view and Chakrabarti’s eastern-origin view are given beside it. I kept “probably” throughout.

Material is thin: sections are about 1,100–2,000 characters; beliefs leans on the Vedic article’s Kuru and Śrauta passage, framed as an interpretation. The 10–15% figure and the drinking-ware forms come from the Vedic article’s archaeology section.
The Iron Age article dates PGW 1300–300 BCE; Tewari/Suraj Bhan debate on early iron taken from it.

Indus Valley Civilisation, Kuru kingdom, Panchala, Mahajanapadas and Northern Black Polished Ware are named in full for encyclopedia links. Spelling “Ahichhatra” used throughout (the article also has “Ahichatra”).
